The fund has secured R3.89 billion, about US$239 million, from development and commercial investors including DBSA, RMB Ventures, Standard Bank, Nedbank and New GX Capital.

Airnergize Capital will focus on commercial scale solar PV, battery storage and other clean infrastructure across Southern Africa and wider African markets.

The fund is also targeting transmission infrastructure, water and wastewater treatment and gas to power projects.

Airnergize Capital has reached the final close of its debut clean technology fund at R3.89 billion, equivalent to about US$239 million, with the investment platform targeting commercial scale infrastructure opportunities across Africa.

Airnergize Capital operates as the clean technology investment arm of South Africa’s New GX Capital, a black owned and controlled investment group. The fund is focused on established infrastructure opportunities with the potential to scale, rather than early stage technology ventures.

Related news: Africa’s cement industry and the push for energy security

The fund has been structured with support from development and commercial financial institutions. The Development Bank of Southern Africa has committed R240 million, with additional capital provided by RMB Ventures, Standard Bank, Nedbank and New GX Capital.

Airnergize Capital said its initial investment focus will be on commercial and industrial solar PV and battery storage assets, with investments expected to build on the activities of Sustainable Power Solutions Africa, its portfolio utility company.

The investment strategy extends beyond renewable generation and storage. The fund is also targeting electricity transmission related infrastructure, including projects intended to help address grid constraints and unlock renewable generation capacity under South Africa’s Independent Transmission Programme.

Water and wastewater treatment infrastructure and gas to power supply networks are also included in the fund’s investment pipeline.

The fund’s final close comes as South Africa and other African markets seek increased private sector investment in electricity generation, transmission, energy storage and essential infrastructure.

Author: Bryan Groenendaal
